Breaking: Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction.
  • These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yet trying for it may still be disastrous.

Recent findings suggest that many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN, “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.”.

These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks.

These ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash fresh competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia.

In a recent development, amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is vital because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology.

According to recent reports, I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm.

RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper, statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians, a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity).

Industry observers note that recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The company’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company confirmed a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028.

It has been revealed that but do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns. This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs.

It has been revealed that such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized, “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation.

This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s at the moment receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.Objection #2: Superintelligence Might Not Be ComputableThere’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s key to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.Penny Gray PhotographyObjection #3: Alignment Isn’t Hard (Given the Right System Design)Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. Recent findings suggest that claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.

Sources indicate that an intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.

Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.

Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s presently receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.

According to recent reports, there’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.

We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.

According to recent reports, but this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.

In a recent development, we cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.

A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.

In a recent development, at the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s important to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.

Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.

In a recent development, last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky swiftly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.

To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a new instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”.

Industry observers note that in a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

Though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the manufacturer’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”.

In a recent development, these examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.

Sources indicate that using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.

In the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.

I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

The misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.

Sources indicate that consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its owners because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted aims for achieving long-term objectives.

According to recent reports, the implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.

According to recent reports, even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the company judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.

This fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

According to recent reports, what’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”.

Google will make AI agents use latest gateways to reach Gmail and Drive

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that google has made its Workspace MCP servers and CLI generally available and states AI agents must use them instead of existing REST APIs from February 1, 2027. Every call is checked against manufacturer policies, sensitive actions need user confirmation, and a new addendum bars AI tools from training on Workspace data.

In a recent development, google will require AI agents to reach Gmail, Drive and other Workspace apps through new, dedicated gateways, it noted on Tuesday. Regular apps can keep using Workspace’s existing APIs, but agents must switch by February 1, 2027.

The gateways are Workspace MCP servers, which use a common standard for linking AI tools to apps, and a command-line tool. Both are now generally available. Google put an early CLI version on GitHub in March.

According to recent reports, google indicates its APIs were built for apps that work at human speed, where a valid login meant the user wanted the action. Agents act on their own at machine speed. So every request now gets checked against organization permissions and data-loss rules.

In a recent development, agents can draft emails and summarise documents on their own. But they need a person’s sign-off before sending email, changing Drive sharing or making bulk edits.

Sources indicate that each agent also needs its own sign-in ID with tight limits and usage quotas. Google already gives its Gemini coworker agents their own accounts. It will begin billing for that usage on April 1, 2027.

According to recent reports, A latest AI Tools Addendum adds rules on data. AI tools cannot use Workspace data to train models or build rival services, and cannot scrape it. They must also delete it when a user disconnects.

It has been revealed that google also tells developers to screen for prompt injection, hidden commands in emails or files that can hijack AI agents. Some controls are still to come, including letting users see and revoke agents’ access themselves.

According to recent reports, other firms are drawing lines too. In October, Charles Schwab said it blocks outside agents from moving client money.

  • Apple’s iPad lineup is incredibly strong, and two standout options are the iPad Air and iPad Pro.
  • Bonus pick: The all-latest iPad mini is up to $100 off for Black Friday as well.
  • Apple updated the iPad Air earlier this year, bringing the M4 chip for improved performance along with 12GB of RAM, up from 8GB in the previous generation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple’s iPad lineup is incredibly strong, and two standout options are the iPad Air and iPad Pro. If you’re trying to decide whether the iPad Pro is worth the extra cost this holiday season, here’s everything you need to know.

Bonus pick: The all-latest iPad mini is up to $100 off for Black Friday as well.

Apple updated the iPad Air earlier this year, bringing the M4 chip for improved performance along with 12GB of RAM, up from 8GB in the previous generation.

Recent findings suggest that the iPad Air is available in 11-inch and 13-inch screen sizes, and uses an LCD display with a 60Hz refresh rate. This means it doesn’t offer OLED or ProMotion, unlike the iPad Pro. It uses Touch ID for biometric authentication, supports the Magic Keyboard and Apple Pencil Pro, and offers the full iPadOS multitasking experience.

Industry observers note that the iPad Air is available in four colors: blue, purple, starlight, and space gray. It starts at 128GB of storage and can be configured up to 1TB.

The iPad Pro is the best iPad money can buy. It’s powered by Apple’s M5 chip and offers many advantages over the iPad Air.

It has been revealed that the biggest difference is the display technology. The iPad Pro is available in 11-inch and 13-inch sizes and uses Apple’s Ultra Retina XDR display with tandem OLED technology. This means it offers deeper blacks, better contrast, and higher brightness than the LCD screen found in the iPad Air.

Sources indicate that the iPad Pro also supports ProMotion with adaptive refresh rates up to 120Hz. This means scrolling, animations, Apple Pencil interactions, and more will be significantly smoother.

In a recent development, contrary to what the naming implies, the iPad Pro is also noticeably thinner and lighter than the iPad Air. The 11-inch iPad Pro measures 5.3mm thick, while the 13-inch model is even thinner at 5.1mm.

The iPad Pro offers Face ID instead of Touch ID, Thunderbolt connectivity, a four-speaker audio system, and nano-texture display options with the higher-end configuration.

Industry observers note that for most people, the iPad Air is the right choice. It delivers the entire iPad experience, excellent performance, and comes in four fun colors and two different screen sizes.

Sources indicate that the iPad Pro is the best iPad you can buy, but it’s overkill for most people. Don’t get me wrong, I love my iPad Pro. If it’s in your holiday budget, it’s a fantastic choice. I can’t overstate how impressive the tandem OLED display is. It’s significantly better than the LCD screen on the iPad Air. It’s also great having Face ID in the iPad form factor.

The iPad Pro is slightly more tempting at its current sale price, with the mid-range 13-inch model at an impressive $350 off.

Still, both the iPad Air and iPad Pro run the same iPadOS experience, and that’s why I think the iPad Air is the better value for most people. What do you think? Let us know down in the comments.

You can now DM Meta’s Muse on Instagram to turn saves into plans

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (301 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Meta has added its Muse AI agent to Instagram direct messages, inviting users to send it a DM to turn saved posts into plans, such as a trip.
  • Meta’s Muse AI agent can now be messaged in Instagram DMs, where it can turn posts users have saved into looks.
  • Muse released in the US in September as an agent that books, buys and negotiates for consumers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meta has added its Muse AI agent to Instagram direct messages, inviting users to send it a DM to turn saved posts into plans, such as a trip. Muse already worked in its own app, in WhatsApp and on Instagram profiles, and Meta claims it does not read private messages unless users allow it, though Reuters reported staff found it reading encrypted chats.

Meta’s Muse AI agent can now be messaged in Instagram DMs, where it can turn posts users have saved into looks. Meta confirmed the change through Muse’s own Instagram account on Tuesday, using a long-planned trip as the example.

Muse released in the US in September as an agent that books, buys and negotiates for consumers. It works in its own app and in WhatsApp, and later that month users could add it to their Instagram profiles.

The DM option puts Muse where the saved posts already sit. Meta has not stated which countries get it. Beyond the US, Muse is live in Canada and has rolled out in Australia, and it reached the UK this week.

Messaging Muse does not give it access to private chats. Meta’s privacy page claims Muse does not read private messages unless consumers allow it through a connector.

Industry observers note that yet Reuters reported last week that Meta staff found Muse reading encrypted messages. Meta called those isolated incidents.

Sources indicate that owners can also make Muse ask before it sends messages or buys anything. In September, though, a YouTuber said Muse shared his address with a Facebook Marketplace buyer before asking him. Meta said it was looking into it.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you.
  • I first got into the driver’s seat of the Ioniq 5 a couple of years back and came away impressed by its futuristic aesthetics and loaded suite of tech features that really added value to its bottom-line cost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, despite new competition, the 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 5 remains one of the most efficient, well-rounded electric crossovers you can buy. While its cabin styling is starting to feel a bit dated, its standout real-world efficiency and spacious interior gives it broad appeal.

Efficiency improves in a major way.

Plenty of legroom and trunk space.

Sharp 360-degee cameras make parking a breeze.

Charming stacked headlight design.

Interior is starting to look boring.

Sources indicate that why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

I first got into the driver’s seat of the Ioniq 5 a couple of years back and came away impressed by its futuristic aesthetics and loaded suite of tech features that really added value to its bottom-line cost. At the time, it stood out as one of the easiest electric crossovers to recommend, easily one of the best electric cars for the money.

Industry observers note that fast-forward to today, and I feel a bit differently after driving more than 80 EVs this year alone. While there's more competition in the compact crossover SUV segment now than ever, car shoppers can’t overlook the $50,815 as-tested price attached to the 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 5 AWD Limited I tested.

Sure, I’ve driven compelling rivals like the Ford Mustang Mach-E, Kia EV6, and the newer Subaru Trailseeker, but you can’t count out the Ioniq 5 just yet. Here’s why.

It has been revealed that I drove the 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 5 for a total of 142.3 miles, reaching an impressive 3.9 mi/kWh throughout that time. Not only is that a marked improvement over the 3.3 mi/kWh average I got when I tested the 2024 model, but it also easily outpaces rivals like the 2026 Subaru Trailseeker and the 2027 Rivian R2.

The Ioniq 5 really shines around town, hitting mostly local roads with stop-and-go traffic and reaching a peak short-distance efficiency of 5 mi/kWh. On longer highway drives, it’s still pretty efficient with a best output of 3.8 mi/kWh. This improvement is important because while Hyundai rates it for 259 miles on a full charge, my 3.9 mi/kWh average translates to roughly 328 miles of real-world range from its 84 kWh battery.

Unfortunately, I couldn’t charge it at home because it didn’t come with a charger, nor did I have an adapter to connect my older J1772 charger. Despite this, adopting Tesla’s NACS charging port makes public charging far more accessible — and Hyundai claims it can add 178 miles of range in just 15 minutes on a 350kW DC fast charger.

2026 Subaru Trailseeker Touring.

Best long distance driving efficiency.

Best short distance driving efficiency.

Recent findings suggest that one of the biggest surprises during my week with the 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 5 wasn't just how smoothly it drove — it was how little energy it used doing it. Again, I can’t stress enough how impressive the 3.9 mi/kWh overall average is, which puts it squarely among the most efficient electric crossovers in its class, especially for a dual-motor AWD model.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Sources indicate that usually, hitting numbers near the 4 mi/kWh mark is reserved for more aerodynamic models like the Lucid Air — or smaller, lighter crossovers like the Subaru Solterra and Toyota bZ. Seeing a boxy SUV deliver this kind of real-world mileage proves how much Hyundai has refined the Ioniq 5's powertrain efficiency.

Despite its compact crossover footprint, the 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 5 feels remarkably open and spacious on the inside thanks to its flat floor and long wheelbase. Both front and rear riders get generous legroom, with back-seat passengers easily stretching out thanks to 39.4 inches of space.

I’m also a fan of Hyundai’s H-Tex seating upholstery, mainly due to how it strikes a great balance between plush cushioning and everyday durability — the seats feel soft and supportive right away, yet the material comes across as rugged enough to handle accidental spills. Around back, that spacious theme carries over into an expansive trunk with a wide opening and plenty of room for luggage, groceries, or bulky gear, offering 26.3 cubic feet of accessible cargo space.

Yes, the design of the 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 5 hasn’t changed much from previous years, but I can’t help falling in love all over again with the headlights. Hyundai’s signature Parametric Pixel design language remains one of its biggest visual cues, anchored up front by its distinctive stacked LED headlights.

In a recent development, unlike conventional round headlights, the slit-like light bars around the hood and squared-off pixel clusters give the front fascia a charming, retro-futuristic edge that still turns heads. Beyond looking great, the crisp LED projector beams cast a bright light pattern on dark roads.

It has been revealed that for a crossover with generous interior space, the 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 5 XRT feels surprisingly agile. Thanks to its low-mounted battery pack and dual-motor HTRAC AWD setup, it delivers instant acceleration off the line and stays remarkably planted through tighter corners and highway lane changes.

The steering is well-weighted without feeling heavy, and I personally prefer setting Hyundai’s regenerative braking paddles to their most aggressive level, which likely contributes to its superb efficiency.

Recent findings suggest that hyundai continues to set the bar for camera visibility in mainstream EVs thanks to how generous it is with premium features. While most EVs come with backup cameras at the very least, the 2026 Ioniq 5 is equipped with a Blind-Spot View Monitor that pops the camera feed directly into the 12.3-inch digital instrument cluster, giving me an unobstructed look at adjacent lanes before I merge.

According to recent reports, that thoughtfulness carries over to the 360-degree Surround View Monitor, which stitches together a sharp overhead view of the vehicle on the center display. Combined with multiple angled curb views and parking distance sensors, maneuvering the Ioniq 5 into tight parking spots is a breeze.

I’ve been in so many different vehicles this year that there are probably fewer than a dozen that stand out for their interior aesthetics. Unfortunately, the Ioniq 5 won’t make the cut this time around. While the exterior still turns heads, the cabin is starting to show its age and feels overdue for a proper refresh.

Recent findings suggest that the dual 12.3-inch display setup and physical climate controls remain intuitive, but the minimalist gray-heavy trim comes off as boring by today's standards. Put it up against newer rivals like the 2027 Rivian R2 — with its warmer materials, cleaner architectural lines, and far more modern cabin styling — and the Ioniq 5's interior starts to look noticeably bland.

As much impressed as I am by the 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 5’s efficiency and sub-$50K as-tested cost, there are quite simply more compelling options out there. If you're willing to stretch your budget just a bit higher, the 2027 Rivian R2 Performance immediately stands out with fresher styling, a far cooler and more modern interior, a spacious frunk, and drop-down rear glass.

On the flip side, if you want to save money without giving up capability, the 2026 Subaru Trailseeker undercuts the Ioniq 5 on price — while offering way more cargo room, higher towing and roof-rack utility, and the kind of brand recognition that makes it an easier everyday sell.

Even with tougher competition, the 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 5 is still well worth buying. Sure, its cabin is starting to look a bit dated, but its standout 3.9 mi/kWh efficiency, generous rear legroom, and sharp camera tech continue to make it one of the most well-rounded electric crossovers on the road.

In fact, it remains the EV I’m most inclined to recommend in Hyundai’s entire lineup, striking a sweet spot that neither the smaller Kona Electric nor the pricier three-row Ioniq 9 quite matches for everyday versatility.

What importance means here. Each entry is a specific mathematical question. Importance considers the significance of a resolution, centrality within its field, reach across fields, scholarly and historical fame, broader recognition, and scientific or practical impact.

How problems are ranked. LLMs compare pairs of problems. A reliability-weighted model combines those judgments into the ranking, with calibration across model families. The model-family weights are OpenAI 1.00, Claude 1.00, GLM 0.95, and DeepSeek 0.90. These are modeling choices, not measured probabilities of correctness.

What a rank means. Nearby ranks can be uncertain. The expanded entries include available ranking ranges and comparison counts. Filtering or alphabetizing the directory preserves every problem’s rank in this edition.

Diagnostics from the preceding source fit. After the reported resolutions, edition ranks were compacted without a latest numerical fit. The displayed uncertainty ranges and comparison counts come from the preceding fit of 1,280 targets; the current eligible pool contains 1,122. These diagnostics were not recomputed for the smaller pool.

In a recent development, related and nested problems. A substantial subproblem or generalization may receive its own rank when it has independent mathematical standing. Families identify narrow groups of related questions; an implication alone does not merge their families. The ranking process checks family crowding, including a diagnostic retaining the highest-ranked member of each family. Family membership does not itself change scores, impose a quota, or create an automatic penalty.

Recent findings suggest that MCP is the open standard Anthropic launched two years ago to link AI agents to outside apps and data. Servers built on it already list the tools Claude can use. With skills, they can also ship step-by-step guides and best practices, which Claude loads only when needed.

Two other features are now generally available. Tasks lets a server run long jobs in the background while Claude keeps working, which ZoomInfo uses for deeper research. Elicitation lets a server pause and ask the user for input.

It has been revealed that gitHub, for example, makes users type a repository’s name before an agent deletes it. Supabase confirms costs before creating a paid project. A fourth feature, File Uploads, will soon let Claude send PDFs, spreadsheets and images to servers.

In a recent development, the features are part of MCP, so servers that support them also work in other compatible apps. Anthropic says MCP now sees over 700M SDK downloads a month. In August, OpenAI and four rivals agreed on a standard for packaging skills and MCP servers.

Skills carry risks, too. That same month, researchers found malicious agent skills that stole passwords and keys after about 1.7 million installs.

Terrestrial networks cannot reach every location. Oceans, remote regions, and disaster zones often remain without coverage. 5G non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by using satellites and high-altitude platforms. Introduced in 3GPP Release 17, NR-NTN keeps evolving through Releases 18, 19, and 20. Satellite links bring latest challenges. Zhang has put in $100M of his own money, Bloomberg reported. Its first product, Time Portal, lets agents browse the web as it was at past dates, so they can practise forecasting without seeing the outcome.

Three of xAI’s co-founders have released Epochal, a startup that wants to teach AI to forecast events. Guodong Zhang, Zihang Dai and Manuel Kroiss revealed the firm and its first product on Tuesday.

In a recent development, zhang has put in $100M of his own money, Bloomberg reported. No other investors have been named.

All of xAI’s co-founders have since left the firm, as Elon Musk rebuilds it after its merger with SpaceX. Another co-founder, Igor Babuschkin, raised $1.1bn for his own startup, River AI, in August.

Today’s AI models learn from an internet where they can already see how things turned out, Epochal says. People, by contrast, have to make choices before they know the result.

Its first product, Time Portal, lets AI agents browse the web as it looked at any moment over the past 30 years. Epochal states it covers more than 1 trillion pages, down to the minute on busy sites. A matching Linux sandbox sets its clock, software and downloads to the same date, so agents cannot spot the trick.

To test it, Epochal ran forecasting agents on 347 live questions from prediction markets Kalshi and Polymarket. Weeks later, it replayed the same questions through Time Portal. In its own test, the replayed forecasts closely matched the originals, with a correlation of 0.98.

Industry observers note that developers can try a limited version for free. Epochal has not stated how it gathered the archive or whether the pages are licensed.

London startup Sequent raises $2.2M to mathematically prove code safe

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (521 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sequent co-founders Ramana Kumar (left) and Charles Cooper at the Alan Turing memorial, after whom the manufacturer’s product Alan is named.
  • Industry observers note that sequent, a London startup that uses mathematical proof to show software obeys its safety rules, has raised $2.2M in pre-seed funding.
  • According to recent reports, its product, Alan, goes after what testing cannot do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sequent co-founders Ramana Kumar (left) and Charles Cooper at the Alan Turing memorial, after whom the manufacturer’s product Alan is named.

Industry observers note that sequent, a London startup that uses mathematical proof to show software obeys its safety rules, has raised $2.2M in pre-seed funding. Frachtis co-led the round with Metaplanet, the investment firm of Skype co-founder Jaan Tallinn, the man who led Anthropic’s 2021 Series A.

According to recent reports, its product, Alan, goes after what testing cannot do. A test checks the cases someone thought to try, while a formal proof highlights the code follows its rules in every case. Writing proofs by hand takes specialists months or years, which has kept the method locked up in fields like aircraft controls.

AI has changed that maths, as the models suit the repetitive grind that proofs demand. With Alan, engineers state their safety rules in plain language, such as no user being able to withdraw more than their balance.

The AI then hunts for the proofs, and a separate checker called HOL4, which uses no AI, confirms every step or throws the proof out.

The company was born from a costly mistake: the CEO, Charles Cooper, who leads Vyper, one of the two main programming languages on Ethereum, in 2021 he accidentally introduced a flaw into its compiler. In July 2023, attackers used that bug to drain more than $60mn from older pools at the exchange Curve and other projects.

It has been revealed that after the attack, Ramana Kumar, a former Google DeepMind safety researcher, offered to help prove the compiler correct. He had formed, having co-created CakeML, a compiler proved correct down to the instructions a computer runs, and the work grew into Sequent, where he is now CTO.

Curve has become the first paying customer. For one type of its pools, Alan has proved that no user can take more than a set limit from depositors, whatever they do and in whatever order.

Whenever the pool’s code changes, “we can prove depositors’ money stays protected by the same limit,” Curve CEO Michael Egorov said in a statement.

Cooper argues the lesson reaches well beyond crypto. Banks and governments have long leaned on keeping their old code private, he indicates. AI-powered attacks are eroding that shield, while cheap proofs hand the advantage back to defenders.

In a recent development, crucially, AI never gets the final word. At DeepMind, Kumar studied how AI finds shortcuts that satisfy a rule’s letter while missing its point. So engineers sign off on every rule themselves, and each proof must pass HOL4, whose core is small enough for experts to inspect line by line.

Alan works on Vyper smart contracts today, with Solidity and Solana support in development and Rust, C, TypeScript, and Python on the roadmap. Early access starts at $99 a month, and the founders’ next target is the Vyper compiler itself, the place where the original flaw lived.

What do we know about the EU Quantum Act ahead of today’s launch

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (487 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • European Commission Executive Vice-President Henna VIRKKUNEN on strengthening security at the EU’s external borders in Brussels, Belgium on Dec.
  • The European Commission presents its long-promised Quantum Act in Strasbourg today, a law meant to turn Europe’s world-class quantum research into companies, factories, and products.
  • Henna Virkkunen, the Commission’s executive vice-president for tech sovereignty, is due to unveil the plan at 10:00 CET, once EU commissioners adopt it at their weekly meeting, but until then, here is what we know.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

European Commission Executive Vice-President Henna VIRKKUNEN on strengthening security at the EU’s external borders in Brussels, Belgium on Dec. 11, 2024.

The European Commission presents its long-promised Quantum Act in Strasbourg today, a law meant to turn Europe’s world-class quantum research into companies, factories, and products.

Henna Virkkunen, the Commission’s executive vice-president for tech sovereignty, is due to unveil the plan at 10:00 CET, once EU commissioners adopt it at their weekly meeting, but until then, here is what we know.

In a recent development, quantum computers use the physics of very small particles to crack problems that today’s machines cannot. The technology promises faster drug discovery and new materials, but it also carries a threat, because a powerful quantum computer could one day break the encryption that protects bank accounts and state secrets.

Recent findings suggest that the law has not been published yet, but leaked drafts show its direction. A version obtained by MLex in October would reserve some public contracts for EU-controlled companies and for firms from countries with mutual deals with the bloc.

Moreover, the same draft would decide who can join Europe’s flagship quantum projects, The Quantum Insider reported. Public buyers in critical sectors would also need systems that can resist quantum code-breaking, known as post-quantum encryption.

The problem the law tries to fix is money, as Europe produces top quantum science and hosts around a third of the world’s quantum startups, according to the Commission’s own figures. However, it attracts only about 5% of global private quantum investment, while the US takes more than half.

Recent findings suggest that today’s proposal is supposed to turn the Quantum Europe Strategy, adopted in July 2025, into law. That strategy wants Europe to lead the world in quantum by 2030 and build more of the tech at home.

“Quantum might sound like science fiction to some, but it is already a reality,” Virkkunen stated when she released that strategy last year.

Recent findings suggest that commission officials have described the Act as a framework rather than a pot of money. Some have even called for consolidation, arguing that too many small quantum firms chase the same customers.

Several member states have not waited for Brussels, like France, which has already placed a €500mn bet on homegrown quantum champions, while startups such as Finland’s IQM run Europe’s only private quantum chip factory.

It has been revealed that the proposal will not change anything overnight, as it must first go to the European Parliament and member states. They will debate and amend the text, a process that usually takes years.

The argument moves straight to Dublin, where the Act will top the agenda at the European Quantum Technologies Conference from 30 November to 2 December.

Industry News: I reviewed the TCL QM64L — and its bright picture, vibrant colors and great gaming features make it a budget standout

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The TCL QM64L is a solid compact budget Mini-LED TV.
  • It has been revealed that why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you.
  • According to recent reports, not everyone has room in their home or dorm room setup for the best 65-inch TVs so finding a smaller, budget-friendly TV that can make movies and shows look great can be challenging.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The TCL QM64L is a solid compact budget Mini-LED TV. It brings great HDR performance, vibrant colors and details, smooth gaming and an improved Fire TV experience. However, you should expect lower black levels, slight blooming and weaker speakers than higher-priced models.

Compact design for small spaces.

Punchy detail in colors, natural skin tones.

It has been revealed that why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

According to recent reports, not everyone has room in their home or dorm room setup for the best 65-inch TVs so finding a smaller, budget-friendly TV that can make movies and shows look great can be challenging. Cheaper TVs can suffer from poor brightness, picture quality, and the smart TV software can be slow and sluggish. The TCL QM64L excels against its rivals in a lot of these categories.

Sporting a sleek, redesigned Fire TV interface and a Mini-LED panel capable of delivering great HDR performance with vibrant colors and natural-looking skin tones, this is a TV that really impresses for its price — $599 for a 65-inch model on Black Friday.

Recent findings suggest that both in my lab testing and hands-on time, the TCL QM64L consistently delivered an enjoyable viewing experience. However, its compact size and budget-friendly price come with some compromises, including poor black levels, slight blooming around bright highlights and bad downward-firing speakers.

The TCL QM64L might not be taking down mid-tier and high-end flagship TVs when you compare its raw specs and our lab test results, but for budget-conscious buyers who want a small compact TV without breaking the bank, it will deliver a great everyday viewing experience.

In a recent development, the TCL QM64L comes in multiple sizes, starting at 50 inches. You can’t buy the 50-inch size directly from TCL, but third-party retailers like Amazon carry the 50-inch size that we reviewed.

According to recent reports, pricing starts at $499 for the 50-inch model, and goes as high as $2,199 for a 98-inch model. When on sale, you can grab the 50-inch model for $429, and the 98-inch model for $1,699. Full pricing for the range can be seen below.

QD-Mini-LED QLED with Full-Array Local Dimming.

Dolby Vision (including Dolby Vision IQ), HDR10+, HDR10, and HLG.

144Hz native refresh rate (HDMI 1, 2), 60Hz (HDMI 3,4).

4x HDMI 2.1, 1x USB-A 3.0, 1x USB-A 2.0, ATSC,SPDIF Digital Audio Optical port.

It has been revealed that like many budget TVs, there’s nothing fancy about the design of the TCL QM64L. The only highlight would be its super thin bezels which come in at around a quarter of an inch thick. It also is made of plastic, with legs that attach at a curved angle to support the bottom of the TV. Up front, there’s a silver lip on the bottom of the panel for the TCL logo.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

I would have loved for this set to feature center-facing legs like some of its competitors, since that would help save even more space in a tight-packed room. This is not a huge dealbreaker, though, since this TV is already so compact.

What I love the most is that TCL packs in four HDMI 2.1 ports. Two of them — HDMI 1 and HDMI 2 — can output 4K at 144Hz, but the other two are capped at 60Hz. Having two 144Hz ports is nice, especially if you’re a gamer, since you can connect two consoles to the TV. The other ports on the TV include one USB 3.0 port and one USB 2.0 port, as well as the ATSC port, and a SPDIF Digital Audio Optical port.

Whether I was watching “Spider-Man: No Way Home” on our lab’s Blu-Ray player, streaming “Cross” on Amazon Prime Video, or watching a simple SDR aquarium video on YouTube, the Mini-LED panel on this TV produced punchy highlights and plenty of visual pop. However, the weaker black levels and some slight blooming in very specific scenes prevent it from delivering what you might get from a more premium and larger TV.

With “Spider-Man: No Way Home” in Filmmaker Mode, the TCL QM64L was great with fine details, natural skin tones and vibrant colors. Tom Holland’s shirt sported a clean, vibrant blue, while fine details like his facial scar and Zendaya’s red lipstick remained sharp. The TV struggled a bit with overall black levels in the details in the Sanctum Sanctorum undercroft, though. The blacks in Norman Osborne’s jacket and the brickwork felt slightly muted and gray.

It has been revealed that in later fight scenes, slight blooming also flared around Spider-Man’s hands as they glowed against dark backgrounds. Punchy silver accents and a shiny gold spider emblem in his Black and Gold Suit, however, proved that the QM64L delivers plenty of visual pop.

When streaming HDR content on Amazon Prime Video, the TCL QM64L wowed me right from the opening seconds in the first episode of “Cross.” Facial textures were impressively rendered, revealing crisp individual strands of beard hair on Cross’s face with that I almost feel the urge to reach out and straighten them.

Sources indicate that to my surprise, the QM64L also handled rapid brightness shifts with ease. It seamlessly transitioned from the shadowy, low-light interior of an interrogation room to a dim, moody tunnel intro and then burst into a punchy, bright outdoor shot of the Washington, D.C. skyline.

Recent findings suggest that finally, switching over to a SDR aquarium video on YouTube, the TCL QM64L continued to impress with its vibrant color handling. As a clownfish navigated through lush pink coral reefs the distinctive white stripe on the clownfish's head popped with crisp, clean brightness against its orange body. This proves that this budget display handles underwater marine scenes with surprising depth and visual punch.

Recent findings suggest that across all tests, the 50-inch TCL QM64L delivers surprisingly impressive picture quality for a budget TV. It brings out crisp fine details, natural-looking skin tones and vibrant colors across SDR and HDR content.

Roku 65-inch Class Select Series 4K QLED (2026).

Vizio Mini-LED Quantum 4K Smart TV 65-inch VQM65-C.

Roku Pro OLED TV 65-inch (Measurements with "Brighter".

I lab-tested the TCL QM64L in filmmaker mode alongside five notable rivals in its class, including the LED-driven Sony Bravia 3 II (65-inch), the the Hisense 65M7SR, the Roku 65-inch Class Select Series 4K QLED (2026), the Vizio Mini-LED Quantum 4K Smart TV 65-inch, and the premium Roku Pro OLED TV 65-inch.

Sources indicate that there’s no doubt that this TV will trail its mid-tier and higher-end competitors in raw benchmarking. It is not going to hit high levels of brightness and color accuracy or performance like a flagship might. However, at this price, it is still a surprisingly bright budget TV.

When it comes to the 10% SDR window measurement, which shows you how bright a TV gets with cable TV and everyday content, the Hisense 65M7SR is the best of the bunch at 466 nits. The TCL QM64L follows at 359 nits, and Sony Bravia 3 II hits 352 nits while the Roku Select Series (334 nits) also comes close to that group. The flagship Roku Pro OLED comes in at 330 nits, while the Vizio Mini-LED Quantum trails the group at 218 nits.

My lab assistant and I personally test every TV across SDR and HDR benchmarks using the 10% window method. For color accuracy, we set the TV to Filmmaker Mode, usually the “best” mode on the TV first. We also disable any ambient light sensors that could skew our meter’s readings.

For our tools, we use the Jeti spectraval 1501-HiRes spectroradiometer to profile the Klein K10-A colorimeter. Once profiled, these work with the Murideo 8K-SIX-G Metal pattern generator and a Tom’s-Guide specific workflow in Portrait Displays’ Calman Ultimate software which helps us determine the TV’s overall brightness and color accuracy across HDR and SDR.

We use a Leo Bodnar 4K Video Signal Lag Tester with the TV’s Game Mode to measure how responsive the TV really is. Once all lab testing is done, we put the TV through subjective testing using a curated selection of films and demonstrates, both on streaming services and on our lab’s Blu-ray player.

Visit our “How we test TVs” guide for a more in-depth explanation on the process.

It has been revealed that for HDR content, the TCL QM64L shines best with 630 nits in our 10% window test. That puts it ahead of every TV in this comparison group except the Vizio Mini-LED Quantum, which leads at 781 nits.

Color accuracy out of the box in Filmmaker mode is where the TCL QM64L is a little weak. Our lab measured a Delta-E score of 3.3, where lower numbers are better.

With SDR color performance, the TCL fell behind everything except the Roku Select Series, although its results are still respectable considering the prices.

When looking at the UHDA-P3 HDR color gamut coverage, which is how most HDR content is presented, the TCL again fell toward the bottom of the back, only just edging out the Roku Select Series once again.

It has been revealed that when it came to the more demanding Rec. 2020 spectrum, the TCL moved up slightly, trailing only the Sony Bravia 3 II and Roku Select Series.

The TCL scored a low result in our input latency tests (13 milliseconds) that put it at the bottom of our test results list, but don't let that fool you: I still enjoyed the gaming experience.

Industry observers note that overall, when battling through a boss fight in Marvel’s Wolverine, I did not experience any lag in my inputs. I also tried playing Sonic Superstars. In this fast-paced game, rolling around collecting coins was fun and super smooth..

Industry observers note that like more premium TVs, TCL bundles in support for VRR, ALLM and Game Accelerator with a Game Bar. All of this meant that when I pressed the menu button on the remote, I could pull up a Game Bar to fine-tune the TV for my gameplay.

Recent findings suggest that features like Game Picture Mode, Shadow Enhancement, and Aiming Aid can spice up the gaming experience. My personal favorite was the Floating Window option, and High Frame Rate mode, which helped me keep track of the frames when playing Marvel’s Wolverine on our lab’s PlayStation 5.

As mentioned earlier, the TCL QM64L has two HDMI 2.1 ports that support refresh rates of 144Hz; in comparison, the Sony Bravia 3 II and the Roku Pro Series both have four HDMI 2.1 ports, but refresh rates are capped at 120Hz.

Recent findings suggest that budget TVs have to make some sacrifices, and one of those is the sound setup. The TCL QM64L sports two 10W speakers on the underside front. With the TV sitting on a table, I didn’t quite enjoy the way it handled audio.

While watching “Spider-Man: No Way Home” on our lab’s Blu-ray player, the dialog presentation felt a little muted and muffled from afar. I was forced to push the volume up into the 20s just to make out dialogue clearly.

Recent findings suggest that listening to "Flower in a Hurricane," from the “Grand Theft Auto 6” trailer, the opening guitars and electronic beats did have some impressive detail and spatial depth. However, as soon as the drum beats kicked in, the bass sounded tinny, hollow, and largely absent.

Pick up one of the best soundbars to upgrade this TV's audio.

It has been revealed that one of my biggest complaints about the previous Fire TV interface found on many budget TVs was how outdated it looked, with a giant ad taking up the top of the screen and the navigation bar awkwardly positioned in the middle. Thankfully, Amazon has given its interface a much-needed makeover. The newly redesigned Fire TV OS that came on the QM64L as an out of the box patch is super clean, speedy, and brings it up to par with what I’ve seen on other SmartTV platforms this year.

Recent findings suggest that the navigation bar now sits at the top of the screen, with clearly labeled sections for profile, search, home, movies, TV Indicates, live, sports and news. It's a much more intuitive layout that I’ve long enjoyed on Google TV and even Samsung’s Tizen OS.

Of course, the ads are still there. Show recommendations and promotional content now take up the space where the old navigation bar used to sit. There's also a dedicated Apps and Channels section, making it easier to jump straight into your favorite streaming services.

The redesigned interface feels more fluid. I frequently dive into the picture settings when testing TVs, and I appreciate how the upcoming menus use a gray background with white highlights to make it easier to see which setting you're adjusting. It's a small change, but one that makes the interface feel considerably more polished.

According to recent reports, this TV also has a cool ambient mode that displays artwork when you're not actively watching something. It's a nice touch that gives the QM64L a little more personality when it's not in use. I love it, and I am sure students putting this TV in a dorm room will too.

The remote included with this TV is nothing fancy. While it is backlit, it has the same standard layout as many remotes that come with TCL’s other TVs. I like the dedicated play and pause button, as well as the buttons for accessing the settings, and Netflix and YouTube. A programmable button would have been nice, but you can’t expect that for this price.

The TCL QM64L is a great 50-inch TV. For budget-conscious buyers, the QM64L delivers where it counts most. Its Mini-LED brightness, attention to fine details, and sleek Fire TV OS helps it stand out as one of the best compact TV values for small living rooms, bedrooms, or dorm setups.

The biggest rival would be the Hisense 65M7SR with its better SDR brightness, slightly more accurate out-of-box color performance, and slightly wider color gamut coverage than the TCL QM64L. While it can't match the TCL's HDR brightness, it's just as compelling an option if you prefer the Roku TV experience and want to prioritize overall color performance over bright HDR.

Recent findings suggest that the QM64L’s budget price tag does come with clear trade-offs like muted, grayish blacks, and slight blooming around bright objects in dark scenes. The downward-firing speakers also deliver hollow audio with muddy dialogue, making a soundbar an essential purchase.

While it is more expensive, the Sony Bravia 3 II still serves as a major step up from this TCL thanks to Sony's superior image processing and color accuracy. Finally, if your main goal is better HDR brightness in a sunlit room, the Vizio Mini-LED Quantum will be for you.

Of course, if budget isn't a strict constraint and you want to completely eliminate blooming with infinite contrast and pristine color, stepping up to an OLED like the Roku Pro Series OLED is the ultimate fix for many of these TVs problems, though it comes at a higher cost.

But, if you're looking for an affordable set under $500, the TCL QM64L could be just the ticket.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that at today’s Microsoft Ignite 2026 keynote, the organization introduced two latest frontier AI models built for what the company describes as “everyday” coding tasks. But there’s a bigger story: what these models might mean for Microsoft’s AI costs and its dependence on OpenAI.

Microsoft claims its MAI Code 2 model shows 96% of Claude Opus 5.5 performance at 5% of Opus 5.5’s price.

Also: Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

Microsoft states MAI Code 2 offers comparable performance to GPT-6.1 Sol or Opus 5.5 at a fraction of the cost. Microsoft’s Code 2 Flash model is comparable to the lower-end GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5, also at considerably lower cost.

It has been revealed that this doesn’t mean that those of us who pay for $100/month subscriptions will suddenly get the equivalent for five bucks. Instead, these are usage-based metrics based on API usage.

According to recent reports, it’s also important to understand that the benchmarks are all Microsoft-provided. Performance numbers may well differ once the models undergo independent performance tests.

According to recent reports, throughout Satya Nadella’s keynote, Microsoft demonstrated slides referencing a wide range of foundation models that are intended to work with Copilot and other Microsoft offerings. Microsoft famously has a multi-billion-dollar investment in OpenAI dating back to 2023, and has built many of its products and services around OpenAI intellectual property.

But now, Redmond is benchmarking its internally built models against Anthropic and OpenAI offerings, and also touting that it’s integrating these latest models as optional choices for GitHub Copilot, Microsoft 365, and Fabric.

Also: 75% of developers I surveyed prefer Claude Code over Codex.

One thing that Nadella made clear in today’s keynote is how central AI is becoming in everything Microsoft does. Nearly all of those AI operations previously involved the organization paying some token fees back to the frontier model providers or customers doing the same thing.

But with high-performing models of its own, Microsoft may become substantially less dependent on outside model providers, especially for the incredible volume of fairly basic and routine AI requests that occur across the firm’s vast product line.

If you think back over the history of agentic work models like ChatGPT Work and Claude Cowork, you may recall that they originated as agentic coding tools. As people adopted the coding harnesses in Claude Code and OpenAI Codex to off-label productivity applications, the AI companies noticed and packaged work-centric agentic tools that were more non-programmer-friendly.

Also: I let ChatGPT Work and Claude Cowork loose on my files – only one made me nervous.

There’s a lot of similarity between a coding agent and a work agent, including understanding a complex environment, using tools to change things, and producing reliable results. Coding turns out to be a very good environment for developing and testing these capabilities, particularly because code output is highly measurable. Coding agents are effective training grounds for non-coding work agents.

Sources indicate that this becomes really interesting in today’s announcement. Along with Code 2 and Code 2 Flash, Microsoft declared MAI Work Flash, which it describes as having been derived from Code 2 Flash. Work Flash can help generate formulas in Excel, work with documents and instructions in Word, track decisions and extract useful information from Teams, and more.

It has been revealed that think about the level of intelligence these tasks are demanding from the AI models. Not that much. As long as the models are good enough, they’ll be good enough.

If Microsoft can reduce its expenses and use reliable models at a much lower price, the company itself will be able to save quite a bit of money across its entire software economy, while at the same time maintaining a deeper level of vertical integration and, therefore, control.

Let’s run some hypothetical numbers. Let’s say a manufacturer is spending $0.01 per AI request, which, with these new models, can drop down to $0.001 per request.

Recent findings suggest that also: Want to try ChatGPT Wallet? Read OpenAI’s liability disclaimer very carefully first.

In a recent development, A company with a daily inference cost of a million dollars (a company like Microsoft, for example) could drop that daily cost to about $100,000. Add that up across a year, and the change in models could save $325 million annually.

A million here, a million there. Pretty soon, you’re talking real money.

According to recent reports, there’s no direct evidence that Microsoft is trying to produce replacement models for the frontier providers’ offerings. But it is an interesting and compelling story if we look at Microsoft developing its own engines for the software it sells.

Microsoft says the numbers it’s reporting at are using a 50% introductory discount. That’s why I measured against $0.001 per request instead of $0.0005 per request above.

Benchmark selection could be cherry-picking. The numbers are impressive. But as we all know, there are lies, damned lies, and benchmark results. I’m fairly sure Microsoft isn’t padding these numbers too much, because it benefits from the latest models more than even its own customers, but still. It’s an open glitch.

According to recent reports, the tech giant also described clearly that these new models are not designed to handle the most challenging agentic and research workloads. Recent findings suggest that plenty of budget cases get the woven look by printing a pattern onto plain plastic. If you’re looking for that style, go for it, but it won’t behave like woven aramid fiber, which lets a case stay rigid and thin without adding much weight.

Even genuine aramid cases aren’t all made the same way. The weave, resin, thickness, and surface finish all change how a case feels in use. PITAKA uses woven aramid fiber in two main weights: 600D and 1500D. Those numbers measure yarn density; the finer 600D weave feels a bit smoother and produces a slightly thinner shell than 1500D. Whatever case you choose, look past the word “premium” and check whether the maker actually spells out what the case is made of.

Most aramid cases stick to plain black and gray. PITAKA’s Fusion Weaving method blends colored fibers and multiple weave styles directly into the shell instead of printing a graphic on the outside. Recent findings suggest that online listings spend almost all their time showing off the back of a case, even though your fingers spend just as much time on the sides, buttons, and bottom edge. Industry observers note that if you use a magnetic charger, wallet, or grip, how the magnets are built into the case matters just as much as the outer material. Sticking a separate magnet ring inside a shell usually adds extra layers and thickness.

In a recent development, PITAKA’s Amber Magnet Film process bonds coated magnets directly with the aramid fiber and resin under heat and pressure. That keeps the magnets enclosed without bulking up the case, which is the kind of detail you won’t spot in a photo but will notice in your pocket.

Spending more on a case doesn’t guarantee it’s better, and plenty of $20 cases are completely fine. Genuine aramid fiber by itself doesn’t guarantee better drop protection either.
