    Arista Networks vs. SentinelOne: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (957 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • By Seena Hassouna – Updated Nov 24, 2026 at 9:23PM EST.
    • Should you prioritize the hardware infrastructure that powers the cloud or the software that protects it?
    • Arista designs the high-speed networking equipment essential for modern data centers, while SentinelOne provides an autonomous security platform.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Seena Hassouna – Updated Nov 24, 2026 at 9:23PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Arista Networks ›.

    Should you prioritize the hardware infrastructure that powers the cloud or the software that protects it? Choosing between Arista Networks (ANET -5.47%) and SentinelOne (S -2.00%) requires balancing established profitability with high-growth potential.

    Arista designs the high-speed networking equipment essential for modern data centers, while SentinelOne provides an autonomous security platform. Both companies are central to the expansion of artificial intelligence, making them notable contenders for investors who want exposure to the future of computing.

    It has been revealed that arista Networks designs and sells cloud networking hardware and software for massive data centers, campus, and routing environments. With over 10,000 global customers, it serves cloud titans and specialized providers, including a strategic reliance on Broadcom (AVGO -3.98%) for merchant silicon. Customer concentration adds a layer of risk to the business, as sales to two specific end customers represented nearly 16% and 26% of total revenue in 2025.

    Sources indicate that in the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached close to $11.9 billion, representing growth of approximately 40.7% compared to the prior year. This expansion was accompanied by a net income of nearly $4.8 billion and a net margin of 40%. The company maintains a strong competitive position among tech stocks by providing the plumbing that powers the world's largest internet companies.

    It has been revealed that as of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio is roughly 3.0x, which measures a company's ability to cover short-term debts with short-term assets. The debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.0x, indicating a very low level of total debt relative to shareholder equity. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was nearly $4.3 billion, which is the cash remaining after paying for operations and equipment.

    Recent findings suggest that sentinelOne provides AI-powered cybersecurity through its Singularity Platform, which detects and responds to attacks across endpoints, cloud workloads, and containers. The company targets organizations of all sizes and works with strategic partners such as N-able (NABL -0.99%) and Cloudflare (NET -1.32%) to reach its customers. Much of its growth is driven by its multi-tenant model, which allows security providers to manage multiple distinct clients through a single interface.

    In the 12 months ended July 31, 2026, revenue reached nearly $1.1 billion, representing growth of nearly 21.1%. Despite this top-line expansion, the company reported a net loss of approximately $340.1 million and a negative net margin of 31%. This reflects the early stage of its growth cycle as it prioritizes market share and platform development over immediate bottom-line profits.

    It has been revealed that based on its January 2026 balance sheet, a current ratio of 1.4x indicates the manufacturer has sufficient current assets to cover its short-term liabilities. The debt-to-equity ratio is close to 0.0x. In the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, free cash flow was nearly $75.9 million, though stock-based compensation represented roughly 388.4% of operating cash flow, meaning reported cash generation is heavily inflated by this non-cash add-back.

    Arista Networks faces significant risks from high revenue concentration among a small number of massive cloud customers. The business relies heavily on Broadcom for essential silicon chips, making it vulnerable to supply chain disruptions. Furthermore, intense competition from Extreme Networks (EXTR -4.97%) and other vendors makes long-term demand forecasting difficult given the rapid evolution of artificial intelligence.

    SentinelOne carries risks related to its history of net losses and accumulated deficits. The manufacturer competes in a crowded cybersecurity market against larger competitors and depends on third-party cloud hosts like Amazon (AMZN -1.21%) to run its services. Additionally, managing rapid growth and navigating the evolving regulatory landscape for artificial intelligence presents ongoing operational challenges for the software provider.

    Recent findings suggest that sentinelOne is cheaper by its P/S ratio, measuring price against sales over the past twelve months. Arista Networks has a lower Forward P/E.

    Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

    Industry observers note that I would buy SentinelOne for 2027, and the case comes down to what has to go right. Arista's price-to-sales ratio already assumes the AI data center buildout continues at full speed, leaving little room for even a modest slowdown from its few giant customers. SentinelOne needs something more achievable: keep growing near 20%, keep widening its positive adjusted operating income, and keep shrinking stock pay as a share of revenue. The latest filing demonstrates all three moving in the right direction, and the firm has acquired AI security firms to sell into the same AI buildout that Arista supplies. The trade-offs are real. SentinelOne's forward earnings multiple is steep, GAAP profit is still a promise, and nearly all its sales run through resellers, two of which carry a large share of revenue. Even so, SentinelOne is the stock with more room to be wrong and still work in 2027. I would keep watch for several quarters to see whether the company hits its targets. Five years on from its IPO, SentinelOne is still early in its public life, and the tailwind behind security spending is strong enough to pay off if the company grows into its multiple. A company named for a lookout deserves a watchful eye, not a substantial bet.

    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nerdwallet ↗ Open Full Page

    How to Get Grants for College

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1070 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdwallet

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that grants are one of the best ways you can pay for your education.
    • Grants can be used for tuition, course materials and other cost-of-attendance expenses.
    • Here’s how to use a college grant and what it can pay for.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that grants are one of the best ways you can pay for your education. It’s free money you aren’t expected to pay back.

    Grants can be used for tuition, course materials and other cost-of-attendance expenses. Some grants, depending on who awards them, require an application or have requirements you must meet before you can get your money.

    Here’s how to use a college grant and what it can pay for.

    There are four main types of grants:.

    Federal grants come from the federal government.

    State grants come from state programs and often can only be used at schools in that state.

    Institutional grants come from your college or university, or even your program or major.

    Private grants come from nonprofits, community organizations and individual donors.

    Industry observers note that to receive a federal grant, you must complete the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA). Most states require the FAFSA for state grants, and a few require a separate state application. You’ll need to complete the FAFSA for each year you’re enrolled in school. You may need to meet certain eligibility requirements, such as income limits, to get some grants. The FAFSA is how you apply for the Pell Grant, which is a financial need-based grant. The FAFSA also determines eligibility for federal work-study, which is a job program rather than a grant.

    Industry observers note that federal aid, including federal grants, typically requires students to meet satisfactory academic progress. This means you have to maintain a minimum grade point average and be on track to finish your degree on time, as determined by your school. Your school also sets how many credits you must take to qualify for grant funding.

    Some grants — typically private or institutional grants — require an additional application that asks for transcripts, letters of recommendation and personal essays. Your school’s financial aid office or the grant provider will have details on applying for specific grants.

    In a recent development, after you submit the FAFSA, you’ll receive a financial aid award letter from each school you applied to, which outlines how much in federal, state and institutional grants you’ve been offered. You must accept your aid to receive it.

    In a recent development, most grants will be disbursed directly to your college or university. Your school will apply the grant money first to tuition, fees and any other charges it bills, such as housing or a meal proposal.

    Sources indicate that in some cases, you may receive more grant money than your school bills, which is the best-case scenario. If that happens to you, any leftover funds will likely be refunded to you. Refund timelines vary by school, so it may take some time to get your money. You can get your refund faster by setting up direct deposit with your school. You can then use the funds for other costs approved by your grant — some examples are detailed below.

    If you have questions about your grant money, contact your college’s financial aid office.

    According to recent reports, grants can help cover cost-of-attendance expenses. Generally, you can use grant money to pay for tuition, textbooks, class materials, transportation, housing and food. Depending on your school’s policies, you can use grant money to cover summer classes or study abroad programs, too.

    Recent findings suggest that some grants come with specific terms about how you can spend them. Check your financial aid award letter or, for a private or institutional grant, the school’s or organization’s website to find specifics.

    Expenses grants aren’t meant for:.

    In a recent development, after your grant is applied to your tuition and school expenses, you can options to fill the gaps between what the grant covers and the total cost of your program. Some options include savings, scholarships, work-study, payment plans, federal student loans or, as a last resort, private loans. By using grants to pay for your college education, you may be able to borrow less.

    Sources indicate that to maximize the grants you’re eligible to receive, enter accurate information on the FAFSA and complete it as soon as you can — some funds are first-come, first-served. Also, don’t limit yourself to federal or state grants — search and apply for as many privately funded grants as you can find.

    Your grant money usually goes straight to your college or university to pay your tuition and fees. Anything that is left over may be disbursed to you for other school-related costs.

    Industry observers note that yes, but it depends on your grant. Housing is part of your cost of attendance, so you can use grant money to pay for off-campus rent.

    Sources indicate that you don’t have to pay back a grant as long as you continue to meet all requirements for the grant, such as staying enrolled. You can use grant money on school and school-related expenses. Some grants may require you to meet eligibility requirements such as a minimum GPA or state residency. If you receive more grant money than your cost of attendance for a given school term, ask your financial aid office if you can put that grant money toward next year’s cost of attendance.

    If you have a federal grant like a Pell Grant, these are examples when you may have to repay all or part of the grant:.

    You withdrew from your program.

    You received enough scholarship money to reduce your federal aid need.

    It depends. You can usually use grant money to buy a laptop. Computers are considered course materials, which fall under cost-of-attendance expenses, so they can be covered by a grant. However, always double-check with the grant provider and your financial aid award letter to ensure that you’re following all restrictions. Whether you can use grant money to cover a laptop depends on your school’s policies and how much grant money you receive.

    If you get more grant money than your school bills you, you’ll likely receive the leftover money to spend on other cost-of-attendance expenses. You can use this money on living costs such as transportation or housing. Grant money often goes mostly toward tuition, so a refund isn’t guaranteed.

    It has been revealed that grant and scholarship money is generally tax-free when you use it for tuition, required fees, books and required class supplies. If you have additional questions, consider talking to a tax professional.

    10 stocks we like better than Tesla ›.

    Tesla (TSLA -0.20%) and Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX -5.65%), Elon Musk's two trillion-dollar companies, took a step closer to merging on Tuesday.

    Both companies have appointed a total of five directors, three from Tesla and two from SpaceX, to guide two special committees to handle merger negotiations.

    In a recent development, the committees have also hired investment banks to develop financial models for the all-stock merger, and a deal could be reached before year's end. If the merger were timely enough, it would also allow SpaceX to be included in the S&P 500 earlier than it would as a stand-alone tech giant.

    It has been revealed that naturally, merging two companies that have the same CEO is easier than merging two unrelated companies. Musk has a majority of SpaceX's voting power and 20% of Tesla's voting power, and could own a majority of the combined manufacturer.

    The full details of Huang's return to Nvidia may never be clear, but President Trump states he played an active role in getting Huang reinstated, telling CNBC that he "convinced" the board to do so.

    That move may have shifted the Overton window significantly in corporate governance, or what's considered acceptable, and also shows that Trump is willing to put his thumb on the scale for his corporate friends, at least when he believes it's in the country's interest, one of which is Musk.

    The dynamics of getting the merger approved versus reinstating Huang are much different, however. Trump just needed to get the board's approval to get Huang back as Nvidia CEO. The Tesla/SpaceX merger, on the other hand, will face a battery of regulatory hurdles to get cleared.

    It has been revealed that china would be an issue in the merger, as Tesla has a significant business there, and SpaceX's technology would likely raise national security concerns. It would have to pass antitrust muster in both the U.S. and Europe, where there could be resistance to creating a firm with a leading position across so many disparate industries. Additionally, Texas Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson has expressed skepticism about corporate concentration and could challenge the combination.

    Still, expectations of corporate governance and President Trump's own ability to influence such decisions have shifted with Huang's reinstatement, which could help the merger go through.

    It has been revealed that while the two companies haven't formally declared an intention to merge, they're likely to go through with it, as all of the interested parties, including Elon Musk, appear to be incentivized by a merger. The deal will serve as a major test for the regulatory apparatus, as antitrust regulators have blocked much smaller deals in the past.

    • 10 stocks we like better than Space Exploration Technologies ›.
    • It has been revealed that any way you define it, I consider Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX -5.65%) the world's best space tech giant.
    • SpaceX launches more frequently than any other space company, too -- 161 times last year versus 21 for Rocket Lab, (RKLB -7.35%), America's second-most frequent launcher (and a launcher of much smaller rockets).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Rich Smith – Nov 24, 2026 at 10:00PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Space Exploration Technologies ›.

    It has been revealed that any way you define it, I consider Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX -5.65%) the world's best space tech giant. SpaceX offers the lowest cost to orbit of any space company -- $74 million for 22.8 metric tons -- or about $3,245 per kilo to low earth orbit.

    SpaceX launches more frequently than any other space company, too -- 161 times last year versus 21 for Rocket Lab, (RKLB -7.35%), America's second-most frequent launcher (and a launcher of much smaller rockets).

    SpaceX has the world's biggest rocket in continuous operation, the Falcon Heavy, with a maximum payload approaching 64 tons, and will soon have an even bigger rocket in rotation -- Starship -- boasting a 100-ton payload.

    It has been revealed that hard on the heels of Starship's partly successful Flight 15, which featured the first-ever tower capture of the spacecraft by Mechazilla after a return to space, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk announced aims to move ahead with an upgrade to Starship. Plans include a 40% increase in the spacecraft's size, which implies a 40% increase in payload to 140 tons and/or a 60% increase in the amount of fuel Starship can carry -- increasing its range and potentially putting the moon within reach.

    SpaceX will also triple the number of Raptor engines on board the spacecraft to nine -- and upgrade their performance.

    It has been revealed that starship V4 will be ~70m long, which is roughly a 40% length increase and allows >60% more propellant load. Engine count will be raised to 9, with 3 more Raptor-Vacuum engines added, and these will be higher thrust V4 engines.

    Space watchers estimate that the latest version of Starship is protected by a total of 18,500 heat shield tiles, which protect the ship as it travels through the atmosphere during reentry. Lose too many of those tiles, and Starship probably blows up. Damage too many of those tiles, and it may take so long to replace them and refurbish the ship that it becomes no longer really "reusable," and more like "recyclable.".

    Which is why this next news is so important.

    According to multiple space accounts I follow that have examined the condition of Starship after its Flight 15, only one heat shield tile appears to have sustained significant damage during reentry. That's a failure rate of just five one-thousandths of one percent (0.005%). And it implies that SpaceX will be both easier and cheaper to refurbish for reuse than previously hoped.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/24/26.

    Musk himself confirmed this in a later post on X, suggesting reflight of a Starship could take as little as "a few weeks" as currently designed. And SpaceX's ultimate goal is still to tweak the design until it guarantees "zero expected refurbishment" and "immediate reusability (like an airplane).".

    Recent findings suggest that yeah, I was going over the whole Starship heat shield earlier today. Overall, it looks great. The engines look great too. Ship 42 could probably be reflown with a few weeks of refurbishment. However, many small fixes are needed to achieve immediate reusability (like an airplane), which requires zero expected refurbishment, apart from scheduled maintenance.

    So what does all this mean to SpaceX shareholders?

    Based on published (and rumored) payload capacities and launch prices, SpaceX's Falcon 9 is at the moment the cheapest non-government-owned rocket in the world.

    It has been revealed that blue Origin's Fresh Glenn, with low operating costs and a massive 45-ton payload, might challenge Falcon if Blue can get it operating consistently. But even if it achieves that goal, Starship is blazing a trail toward $1,000-per-kilogram prices for low earth orbit. A working Starship that costs $10 million to operate and charges $100 million per 100-ton launch would cost barely one-third of Falcon's per-kilogram price -- and half that of New Glenn.

    It would generate roughly 90% profit margins for SpaceX (versus negative margins today, according to data from S&P Global Market Intelligence).

    And it will be even more profitable if SpaceX makes it 40% larger.

    I've remarked it before, and I'll say it again: advantage SpaceX.

They must also modernize their data architectures, including semantic data layers that provide context around their data and intellectual property. Data centers are becoming value centers, driving growth, productivity, speed and intelligence across the enterprise. Now let's start with the results. Starting with ISG. Every AI order is vetted for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance and access to land and power. As I mentioned, each design is bespoke, optimized through multiple iterations with the customer. Through this tight collaboration, we know our customers well and have a high conviction that our backlog will convert to revenue. Our pipeline grew sequentially and remains multiples of our backlog, again, after converting $180 billion over the past 4 quarters. Additionally, our customer base and opportunity pipeline continues to diversify.

    Recent findings suggest that we now have over 7,500 Dell AI Factory customers. Our customer base spans neoclouds, sovereigns and enterprises. Within the neocloud segment, we remain highly selective about the partners we work with and the end customers supporting their demand. The global opportunity is expanding as more data centers are built outside of the United States. Across nearly every top country around the world, there are 2 to 3 sovereign projects. Enterprises were the fastest-growing portion of our opportunity pipeline expansion sequentially, providing further evidence that enterprise AI adoption is gaining traction. Internally, we continue to invest in our capabilities, ensuring we maintain our competitive advantage, deliver value for our customers and position for the substantial opportunity ahead. Moving to traditional servers.

    Revenue was up 235% as demand remained exceptionally strong, supported by multiple growth drivers that are expanding our TAM. Enterprises increasingly recognize that compute is critical to both the growth and the operations of their business. They are buying more compute to accommodate growing workloads, refreshing their installed base and modernizing their data centers to free up power and space to be positioned for the AI era. Sequentially, we are seeing increased demand for CPU-based compute to support AI and inference workloads. Higher content continues to be a long-term secular tailwind. Servers contain more compute value with higher core counts, greater memory and storage capacity, increasing the value of each system.

    Sources indicate that underneath all of this, cyber resilience and security are also driving refresh activity. Much of the installed base requires newly introduced hardware to meet current security and performance requirements. These needs cannot always be addressed through a software patch. We are executing very well in a supply-constrained environment, and we expect to gain share this quarter. Turning to storage. Revenue was up 24% as strong demand for our Dell IP portfolio drove revenue growth and improved profitability. Storage has always been critical as enterprise workloads and data grow. In the AI era, it is becoming even more crucial as data grows at exponential rates. Our storage opportunities are also expanding as AI evolves.

    AI workloads are creating upcoming demand drivers like key value caching, context layers and agents that need to store data, memory and state. For an enterprise, its data is its intellectual property, but siloed and without context, it's just data. Agents need that context, and that's why we've expanded the Dell AI Data Platform with a unified semantic layer and an enterprise knowledge graph. Together, they give nearly every application and agent the same trusted current view of the business without rebuilding context from scratch every query. This lowers token consumption, cuts compute costs and speeds time to production, all while keeping the customers' most sensitive data governed inside their own data center. Our storage offerings continue to expand.

We also continue to see strong demand for unstructured storage, supporting AI workloads with triple-digit demand growth for the third consecutive quarter. PowerStore delivered a record demand and has now grown double digit or better for 10 consecutive quarters. PowerFlex grew double digits for 3 consecutive quarters and data protection delivered double-digit growth.

Our Dell IP performance and accelerating pace of product development give us confidence in the opportunity ahead. Turning to CSG. Revenue grew 3% in a softer PC unit market as the industry adjusts to higher price points. Customers are prioritizing their budgets near term to servers and storage, electing to defer some PC-related refresh. The installed base continues to age, building deferred demand that we expect to refresh in the future. In closing, we continue to deliver a record year with record revenue, EPS, cash generation and capital return to shareholders.

Just trying to understand what might be changing there and what that might mean preliminarily for fiscal year '28, please?

    Industry observers note that david Kennedy: Yes, sure, Erik. Yes, like I said earlier, if you look at our Q4 guide, we're adding more revenue, more margin dollars, more operating margin rate into the guide versus 90 days ago and again versus 180 days ago. We continue to raise the bar there. So you see $23.5 billion into the Q4 guide. That's running its way through.

    According to recent reports, and then look, as we touched on earlier, as we look through the Q3 performance in that 235% growth from traditional server, a nice kind of tailwind mix of North America business in there in terms of the operational execution. We've modeled here that will normalize its way back in. But ultimately, obviously, our ISG operating margins here for Q4 are above the high end of our range. So very strong performance and a good indication of the strength in the P&L.

    Jeffrey (Jeff) W. Clarke: Yes, Erik, I would step back maybe and look at it from an annual basis. If you look at the guidance that we rolled out at the beginning of the year and with the guidance that we just summarized for the year and for Q4, we will have added nearly $58 billion of ISG revenue, $28 billion of that in AI servers and $30 billion of that in core servers or traditional servers, networking and storage. And in doing so, our operating income has expanded a little over 400 basis points. So the macro theme as we've grown significantly in AI, the core business continues to grow, and you're seeing that expansion.

    And I think with the prospects of the demand durability, the demand outlook that we see going forward and the leverage of our operating decisions that we're making with modernization, we can continue to see performance in that range.

And then I also believe in your prepared remarks, you talked about liquid cooled networking and storage. As that gets added at the rack level, how material can that be for Dell? We have priced Vera Rubin with the expected delivery date with all of our customers when their availability of buildings and power, et cetera, are lined up. The opportunity to attach networking and storage, I think we've been consistent on is an opportunity for margin improvement across our businesses. We continue to focus on that. We continue to see nice attach rates. We still have work to do.

    Industry observers note that I look at our -- if Arthur Lewis was in here from our ISG business, we would talk about how do we grow our storage business inside all of these accounts. That's what we continue to focus on. I just made reference about all of the newly introduced storage opportunities that exist around AI and agentic AI. That's where our focus is with our storage solutions at an individual software-defined storage layer at an appliance layer and at a rack level for all of these large deployments.

    Again, a lot of agentic AI is going to be done in the enterprise, where we have a large footprint today, where we have significant coverage today and where our teams are focused on delivering the right products for enterprise scale as well as driving the rack scale products for the largest clusters and neoclouds in the world.

    Operator: And we'll move to our next question from David Vogt with UBS.

    Industry observers note that david Vogt: Maybe, Jeff, major picture thematically, can you kind of share your perspective on the server market, particularly if we start to see some deflation or maybe steady pricing for DRAM and NAND? And what that means from a customer demand perspective, pricing? Presumably, there are customers on the sideline given the rapid increase in pricing that we've seen across the CPU server market. But would love to kind of get your perspective in terms of where you think pricing goes, demand? I know it's a difficult question, but also sort of configurations and maybe specifications in an environment that's maybe not as inflationary from a component perspective.

    According to recent reports, jeffrey (Jeff) W. Clarke: Well, I'll start with not as inflationary is still a cost increase to our customers in the form of price. And given the significant inflation that's occurred over the past year, even a moderating inflationary number still leads to higher-priced products for our customers. From a macro view, when we look at the supply picture and our supply outlook, there's nothing that suggests that we're going to see price declines in enterprise NAND and DRAM for servers. The demand for those categories of memory continues to be way ahead of the supply. As more DRAM wafer capacity is set forth for GPUs and specifically building HBM, it comes at the expense of all other types of memory.

    In a recent development, we think that crunch continues clearly into '27. And while the rate of inflation won't be the same as we saw in '26, we still believe the market is inflationary. Customers are spending their budgets today. We don't -- I don't know of a customer that's on the sideline that doesn't buy as much as they used to, but I'd also tell you that server they're buying today, if it's a 17G or an 18G server from us, is significantly more capable than the thing that it's replacing. So if you were to take a 14G that we sold 5 years ago, 4 years ago, and it's being retired, that product was $7,500, give or take.

    While today's 18G product will be more expensive than that, it replaces 12 to 14 of them. The consolidation rate is significant and customers are benefiting from that. And while they're tying all of the questions together, while that may mean fewer units, it's a more capable machine, and that is what's being deployed in small businesses to the largest corporations in the world to meet their needs. But customers aren't on the sideline in servers. It would be different if we were talking about PCs. I think companies are deferring their PC purchases to ensure they have the infrastructure to work in what is going to be a very disruptive era with agentic technology really reinventing companies.

    And that's what we see happening in the marketplace. So do I think the rate of increase slows? Yes. Do I still think that a significant price implication to our customers? Yes, because a smaller percentage on a large number is still a lot of dollars. Customers are spending their budgets. We see them active in the marketplace, and we believe that will continue into '27.

So for investment-grade customers, the originations growth we've seen in PCs, storage and servers, up 55% in Q3. So you can see there's an appetite and the need to get infrastructure built out. So even in a budget crunch in the near term, the ability to turn CapEx into OpEx and understand what that looks like is a differentiated capability that we have in the marketplace. And I think our customers have appreciated the flexibility and being able to take advantage of that as part of their IT build-out.

It's not the largest portion of our traditional server business, which is our traditional enterprises and traditional applications, the things that we've talked about before. When I think about these servers going into these new workloads, it is across neoclouds who are deploying them that's in the financial services market.

    It's in the EDA market, it's in the semis market, high-frequency traders, pharma, et cetera, they're very advanced in their AI deployments. They are driving agentic AI across their enterprises. And we believe that market continues to grow as the next iteration or evolution of agentic takes place, which is recursive learning. All of that drives more compute. More agents, more compute. The harness is essential to this. And the harness and the work that the harness does is really a CPU task. It's these things about how you manage containers, how do you manage sandboxes, manage I/O, how do you orchestrate that workload, which is CPU-driven is what we're talking about here.

    And I referenced earlier, those types of servers are roughly twice the ASP as an enterprise-class server running an enterprise workload. The margins in those classes of devices as all of our -- across our server portfolio is well within our product-by-product internal marks that we make for our server products, and we feel very comfortable about that business and the prospects of growth are significant.

    Paul Frantz: All right. And Jeff, please close it out.

    Jeffrey (Jeff) W. Clarke: Sure. Thanks, Paul, and thanks, everyone, for joining us today. Our full year revenue guidance of $202 billion and non-GAAP diluted EPS of $29.68, nearly up 190%. We head into FY '28 with strong momentum and confidence in our ability to continue creating long-term value for shareholders. Thanks again for your time today. Happy Thanksgiving to everyone.

    Operator: This concludes today's conference call. We appreciate your participation. You may disconnect at this time.
